context.heading: Darkness could not get hold of it
context.body: The verb in v. 5 is katalambanō, which can mean "grasp" in the sense of understanding or "seize" in the sense of overpowering. John may intend both: the darkness neither understood the light nor managed to put it out. The same verb returns in 12:35, where darkness tries to "overtake" people.

context.heading: The Son who explains the Father
context.body: "Has made Him known" translates exēgeomai, to lead out, narrate or explain in full, the root of our word "exegesis." No one has seen God, as Moses learned (Exodus 33:20). Jesus, who shares the Father's closest place, is God's own explanation of Himself. Many of the earliest manuscripts read "the one and only God" here, which makes the claim even stronger.

context.heading: Which lamb did John mean?
context.body: John the Baptist calls Jesus the amnos, "lamb," of God. His hearers could think of the Passover lamb (Exodus 12), the lambs offered every morning and evening at the temple (Exodus 29:38–42) or the servant led like a lamb to slaughter (Isaiah 53:7), and he may mean all of these. And this lamb deals with the sin of the whole world, not Israel alone.

theology.title: God was never alone
theology.body: "The Word was with God, and the Word was God" holds two truths together: the Word is distinct from the Father, yet fully God. This chapter lays the groundwork for the doctrine of the Trinity, and it is why Christians confess Jesus as "God from God" rather than a created messenger.

theology.title: Sinai's grace in a person
theology.body: When God showed Moses His glory, He named Himself "abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness" (Exodus 34:6). John's "full of grace and truth" (v. 14) echoes those words. The law given through Moses was itself a gift, but in Jesus the character God described at Sinai walks among us in person.

theology.title: Jacob's ladder comes to earth
theology.body: Jesus promises Nathanael that he will see angels ascending and descending on the Son of Man (v. 51), the image of Jacob's dream at Bethel (Genesis 28:12). Jacob, the deceiver, met God there; Nathanael is "an Israelite in whom there is no deceit" (v. 47). Jesus Himself is now the place where heaven and earth meet.

application.title: Invite instead of argue
application.body: Nathanael opens with a put-down: nothing good comes from Nazareth. Philip does not debate the point. He simply says, "Come and see."
application.question: Who are you trying to argue into faith when you could simply invite them to come and see?

application.title: The man who kept saying "I am not"
application.body: John the Baptist denies being the Christ, Elijah or the Prophet, then lets his own disciples walk off after Jesus (v. 37). He measured success by where people ended up, not by who got the credit.
application.question: Where are you quietly trying to be the center of a story that should point to someone else?

application.title: The first question Jesus asks
application.body: Jesus' first words in John's Gospel are a question: "What are you looking for?" (v. 38).
application.question: If your calendar and bank statement answered that question for you, what would they say you are looking for?

context.heading: "Woman" and the hour
context.body: Gynai, "woman," was a respectful address in Greek, not a cold one; Jesus uses it again from the cross when He provides for His mother (19:26). Still, "What is that to you and to Me?" sets a gentle distance. His "hour" has not yet come. That hour, mentioned again and again (7:30; 12:23; 13:1), is His death and glorification.

context.heading: Zeal that will eat Him up
context.body: The disciples recall Psalm 69:9: "Zeal for Your house will consume Me." Zēlos is burning devotion, and the verb behind "consume" means to devour. Psalm 69 is the prayer of a righteous sufferer, quoted again at the cross (19:28–29; Psalm 69:21). The zeal that cleared the temple will cost Jesus His life.

context.heading: A market in the courts
context.body: Pilgrims needed approved animals and coins, so the trade met a real need; the problem was that it seems to have filled the outer court, where Gentiles could pray. Zechariah 14:21 promised a day with no traders in the Lord's house. John tells this event early, while the other Gospels place a cleansing in the last week; some think it happened twice, others that John arranged it by theme.

theology.title: The generous God of the new age
theology.body: The prophets pictured the coming age with wine overflowing: mountains dripping sweet wine (Amos 9:13) and a feast of aged wine for all peoples (Isaiah 25:6). Jesus' first sign is not a dramatic rescue but an act of lavish kindness at a village party. It shows the character of the God who is arriving: not stingy, not grudging, saving the best for last.

theology.title: The Lord comes suddenly to His temple
theology.body: Malachi promised that "the Lord you are seeking will suddenly come to His temple," and asked who could endure His coming (Malachi 3:1–2). In Jesus, God arrives in His own house and finds it unfit. His holiness is not a cold rule but a jealous love for true worship, the same love that will lead Him to make His own body the new temple.

application.title: The servants knew
application.body: The head waiter tasted the wine and praised the groom; only the servants who hauled the water knew what had happened (v. 9). Jesus' first miracle was witnessed by the people doing the dull, unseen work.
application.question: Are you willing to keep filling jars no one notices if it means you get to see what Jesus does with them?

application.title: Do whatever He tells you
application.body: Mary's last recorded words in this Gospel are an instruction to others: "Do whatever He tells you" (v. 5).
application.question: Which clear command of Jesus are you currently negotiating with instead of doing?

application.title: Impressed is not the same as trusting
application.body: Many believed because they saw signs, yet Jesus did not entrust Himself to them (vv. 23–25). He knew what fair-weather enthusiasm is worth.
application.question: If God stopped giving you visible answers for a year, what would your faith still be standing on?

context.heading: Wind, breath and Spirit
context.body: In v. 8 Jesus plays on pneuma, which means both "wind" and "Spirit." You cannot see the wind or control it, but you see what it does. "Born of water and the Spirit" (v. 5) probably recalls Ezekiel 36:25–27, where God promises clean water and a new spirit, which explains why a teacher of Israel should have understood (v. 10). Christians read "water" in different ways.

context.heading: The bridegroom's friend
context.body: At a Jewish wedding the groom's friend helped arrange things and stood by on the day; his joy was to hear the groom's voice. The Old Testament calls God Israel's husband (Isaiah 54:5; Hosea 2:16–20). By calling Jesus the nymphios, "bridegroom," John the Baptist quietly gives Him a role that belonged to God.

context.heading: Wrath that remains
context.body: Verse 36 says God's wrath "remains" on the one who rejects the Son. The verb is menō, the same word Jesus uses for abiding in Him (15:4). Wrath is not described as something newly invented for unbelievers but as a condition that stays in place unless the Son removes it. Both eternal life and judgment begin in the present, not only at the end.

theology.title: Love for a hostile world
theology.body: In John, kosmos ("world") usually means humanity organized against God: the world did not know Him (1:10) and later hates His followers (15:18). So the wonder of v. 16 is not that the world is big, but that it is bad, and God loved it anyway. His love is measured by a gift, His one and only Son.

theology.title: Judgment as a preferred darkness
theology.body: God did not send the Son to condemn the world (v. 17). Judgment, in vv. 19–21, is people choosing the darkness they love over the light that exposes them. God is not eager to condemn, yet He takes evil seriously. The light that saves is the same light that reveals.

application.title: Credentials don't count here
application.body: Nicodemus was learned, moral and respected, and Jesus still tells him he must be born from above. The new birth is not an upgrade for the irreligious; it is a necessity for the impressive too.
application.question: Which of your strengths are you quietly counting on to make you right with God?

application.title: Questions after dark
application.body: Nicodemus came at night, perhaps to protect his reputation. Later he would defend Jesus in public and help bury Him (7:50; 19:39).
application.question: What would it cost you to ask your real questions about Jesus in daylight, where people could see?

application.title: Losing followers gracefully
application.body: John's disciples were worried that everyone was going to Jesus (v. 26). John answered, "He must increase, but I must decrease."
application.question: Whose growing success are you secretly resenting, and what would rejoicing in it look like this week?

context.heading: Not sharing a cup
context.body: "Jews do not associate with Samaritans" (v. 9) uses synchraomai, which many scholars think means more precisely "do not use vessels in common." Samaritan utensils were regarded as ritually unclean. When Jesus asks to drink from her jar, He crosses a line any observant Jewish man would have avoided, and she is stunned that He even asked.

context.heading: True worship, not a better mountain
context.body: The woman raises the old dispute: Mount Gerizim or Jerusalem? Jesus answers that the hour is coming for alēthinos ("true, genuine") worshipers. John uses the same word for the true light (1:9), the true bread (6:32) and the true vine (15:1). Real worship is not tied to a holy site but to the Spirit and to the truth now present in Jesus.

context.heading: A title borrowed from Caesar
context.body: The Samaritan villagers call Jesus "the Savior of the world" (v. 42). Sōtēr, "savior," was a title given to Roman emperors, praised as bringers of peace to the world. Outsiders whom many Jews despised give Jesus the widest title anyone gives Him in this Gospel.

theology.title: The seeking Father
theology.body: "The Father is seeking such people to worship Him" (v. 23). God is not waiting for the right people to find the right mountain; He comes looking, as the shepherd who searches for scattered sheep (Ezekiel 34:11). Jesus' detour through Samaria is that search made visible.

theology.title: The fountain Israel forsook
theology.body: Through Jeremiah, God called Himself "the fountain of living water" whom Israel abandoned for cracked cisterns (Jeremiah 2:13). When Jesus offers living water that ends thirst for good, He offers what only God gives. He is greater than Jacob, who could only dig a well.

theology.title: A word that works at a distance
theology.body: The royal official asks Jesus to come down; Jesus simply says, "Your son will live" (v. 50), and the boy recovers at that hour. God's word does what it says, as Isaiah 55:11 promised. The official believes before he sees, and his whole household follows.

application.title: Trips to the well
application.body: Whatever lay behind her five marriages, the woman knew what it was to keep returning to something that never satisfied. Jesus does not shame her; He names her story and offers water that lasts.
application.question: What do you keep going back to every day that has never once left you satisfied?

application.title: Food they didn't know about
application.body: The disciples bring lunch and find Jesus more energized than hungry, fed by doing His Father's will (v. 34). Obedience can nourish, not only drain.
application.question: What part of your week actually feeds you, and how much of it has anything to do with God's will?

application.title: Testimony without credentials
application.body: The woman had no training, only one sentence: "He told me everything I ever did." A whole town came because of it, and then believed for themselves.
application.question: Who needs to hear your one honest sentence about what Jesus has done for you?

context.heading: A verse missing from the oldest copies
context.body: The sick waited for the water to be stirred (v. 7). Older translations include a verse 4 explaining that an angel stirred the water and the first one in was healed. That verse is absent from the earliest manuscripts, so most modern Bibles footnote it; it probably records a popular belief. The man's real problem is clear either way: no one would help him.

context.heading: My Father is still working
context.body: "My Father is working until now, and I am working" (v. 17) uses ergazomai, to work or labor. Jewish teachers generally agreed that God did not stop working on the Sabbath, since He keeps the world running and gives life and death every day. Jesus claims to share that same Sabbath work. His opponents understand the claim perfectly.

context.heading: Searching the Scriptures
context.body: Ereunaō (v. 39) means to search carefully, the way a scholar studies a text. Jesus' hearers were diligent students who believed eternal life was found in the Scriptures. He says the Scriptures testify about Him, so it is possible to study the Bible closely and still miss the person it is about.

theology.title: The Son does the Father's work
theology.body: Giving life and judging belong to God alone: "I put to death and I bring to life" (Deuteronomy 32:39). Jesus says the Son does both (vv. 21–22), not independently but in perfect unity with the Father, so that all should honor the Son as they honor the Father. This is not a junior deity but the Son sharing the Father's own works.

theology.title: Life now, resurrection later
theology.body: Whoever believes "has" eternal life now and has crossed from death to life (v. 24). Yet an hour is also coming when the dead in their tombs will rise to life or judgment (vv. 28–29), echoing Daniel 12:2. God's rescue begins in the present and ends with bodily resurrection.

application.title: Do you want to get well?
application.body: After thirty-eight years, Jesus asks a question that sounds obvious. Long-standing brokenness can become an identity, a routine, even a comfort.
application.question: What broken pattern have you lived with so long that being healed would honestly feel threatening?

application.title: A rule instead of a miracle
application.body: The leaders see a man carrying his mat on the Sabbath, not a man walking for the first time in decades (v. 10). They notice the rule before the rescue.
application.question: When someone around you changes, do you notice the change first or what they did wrong to get there?

application.title: Whose approval runs you
application.body: Jesus says the real barrier to belief is seeking glory from one another instead of from the only God (v. 44). Approval-hunger quietly decides what we can believe.
application.question: Whose approval, if you lost it tomorrow, would hurt more than losing God's?

context.heading: A crowd that wanted a king
context.body: After the feeding, the crowd calls Jesus "the Prophet" promised by Moses (v. 14; Deuteronomy 18:15) and plans to harpazō Him, to seize Him by force, and make Him king. A man who could feed thousands in the wilderness looked like the leader for a revolt against Rome. Jesus withdraws alone. He will be King, but not on terms set by a hungry crowd.

context.heading: Drawn by the Father
context.body: Helkō (v. 44) means to draw or drag; John uses it for hauling a full net (21:11) and drawing a sword (18:10). No one comes to Jesus unless the Father draws them, and later Jesus will draw all people (12:32). Christians differ on how this drawing relates to human choice, some stressing that it always succeeds and others that it can be resisted. All agree no one comes to Jesus on their own initiative.

context.heading: A word that would not soften
context.body: In v. 54 Jesus switches from the ordinary verb for eating to trōgō, a blunt word for chewing or munching. When the crowd stumbles, He makes the language more vivid, not less. Christians differ on how directly this speaks of the Lord's Supper; many note that in this chapter eating and believing run in parallel (vv. 35, 47), with the Supper later giving that faith a visible form.

theology.title: The Father is the true giver
theology.body: "It was not Moses who gave you the bread from heaven, but My Father" (v. 32). Behind every meal in the wilderness stood God, not His servant. Now the same Father gives something greater than manna: His Son, who does not spoil overnight and gives life that does not end.

theology.title: The One who walks on the sea
theology.body: On the dark lake Jesus says, literally, "I am; do not be afraid" (v. 20). In the Old Testament it is God who "treads on the waves of the sea" (Job 9:8) and makes a path through the waters (Psalm 77:19). The feeding and the crossing together echo the exodus, with Jesus doing what Israel's God did.

application.title: Following for the bread
application.body: Jesus tells the crowd they are looking for Him because they ate their fill (v. 26). It is possible to follow Jesus for what He adds to life rather than for Him.
application.question: If following Jesus stopped improving your circumstances, how much of your devotion would still be there?

application.title: Five barley loaves
application.body: Barley was the cheap bread of the poor, and Andrew wonders what one boy's lunch could do for so many (v. 9). Jesus starts with what is handed to Him.
application.question: What small thing do you keep calling "not enough" instead of simply handing it over?

application.title: Nowhere else to go
application.body: When many walk away, Peter does not claim to understand everything; he only knows there is no better place to go.
application.question: When a hard word from Jesus offends you, where exactly do you plan to go instead?

context.heading: No diploma
context.body: "How does this man know letters without having studied?" (v. 15). Grammata, "letters," meant formal learning, the kind gained by sitting under a recognized rabbi. Jesus had no such credentials, and the same charge was later made against Peter and John (Acts 4:13). Jesus answers that His teaching is not His own but comes from the One who sent Him.

context.heading: Judging by the surface
context.body: Jesus points out that they circumcise on the Sabbath when the eighth day falls on it (Leviticus 12:3), so why be angry that He made a whole man well? "Do not judge by appearance" (v. 24) uses opsis, the face or outward look of a thing. Right judgment looks past the surface to what God is actually doing.

context.heading: Look it up
context.body: The Pharisees tell Nicodemus to "search" (ereunaō, the word from 5:39) and see that no prophet comes from Galilee (v. 52). Yet Jonah came from Gath-hepher in Galilee (2 Kings 14:25). John's readers would also catch the irony of vv. 41–42: the crowd says the Christ comes from Bethlehem, not knowing that Jesus was born there.

theology.title: Patient with an unbelieving family
theology.body: Even Jesus' brothers did not believe in Him (v. 5). Yet one of them, James, later saw the risen Lord (1 Corinthians 15:7) and became a leader in the Jerusalem church (Acts 15:13). God's patience reaches people who think they know Jesus best and believe Him least.

theology.title: The Father keeps the clock
theology.body: They tried to seize Him, "but no one laid a hand on Him, because His hour had not yet come" (v. 30; also v. 44). Hostile leaders, armed officers and a divided crowd cannot move God's timetable. The cross will come, but at the hour the Father appoints, and not a moment before.

application.title: The people who knew Him best
application.body: Jesus' brothers grew up with Him and still treated Him as a project to promote (vv. 3–4). Familiarity can make us the last to see clearly.
application.question: Has growing up around church made it easier or harder for you to take Jesus seriously?

application.title: Hear them first
application.body: Nicodemus asks a simple question: does the law condemn a man without first hearing him (v. 51)? The council answers with a sneer instead of a reason.
application.question: Whose story have you already made up your mind about without ever hearing it from them?

application.title: Wanting to be seen
application.body: His brothers urge Him to show Himself to the world, but Jesus goes up to the feast quietly (v. 10). He refuses to let publicity set His agenda.
application.question: What good thing are you doing mainly because people will see it?

context.heading: A treasured story with a wandering place
context.body: The account in 7:53–8:11 does not appear in the earliest Greek manuscripts, and in later ones it shows up in different places, including after Luke 21:38. Most scholars, including many evangelicals, conclude it was not part of John's original Gospel, though many think it preserves a true memory of Jesus. Nothing in Christian teaching depends on it alone, and modern Bibles mark it so readers can see the evidence.

context.heading: Free people who were never slaves
context.body: Jesus promises that the truth will eleutheroō, "set free" (v. 32). His hearers reply that Abraham's children have never been slaves, despite Egypt, Babylon and Rome. Jesus means a deeper slavery: whoever sins is a slave of sin (v. 34). In a household a slave could be sold, but a son belonged for good (v. 35).

context.heading: A murderer from the beginning
context.body: Anthrōpoktonos (v. 44), "man-killer," is a rare and blunt word. It likely recalls the serpent's lie that brought death in Eden (Genesis 3) and Cain's murder of his brother (1 John 3:12). Jesus, Himself a Jew, is speaking to particular opponents who want to kill Him, not passing judgment on the Jewish people as a whole.

theology.title: The promise Abraham waited for
theology.body: "Abraham rejoiced to see My day" (v. 56). God had promised Abraham that all nations would be blessed through his offspring (Genesis 12:3; 22:18). Jesus presents Himself as the goal of that promise and as the eternal "I am" who existed before Abraham was born. God's covenant faithfulness runs straight from Genesis to this conversation.

theology.title: Mercy that does not excuse
theology.body: "Neither do I condemn you. Go, and from now on sin no more" (v. 11). Whatever its manuscript history, the scene fits the Jesus of every Gospel: He refuses to condemn, and He refuses to call sin harmless. God's grace is not a shrug; it is a pardon that sends a person into a new life.

application.title: Put the stone down
application.body: One by one, from the oldest down, the accusers walk away (v. 9). Nobody in the circle was qualified to throw first.
application.question: Whose failure are you holding like a stone, waiting for the right moment to throw it?

application.title: Slaves who feel free
application.body: The crowd insisted they had never been enslaved. Addiction rarely feels like slavery from the inside.
application.question: What habit would you say you could quit anytime, but somehow never have?

application.title: Staying in the word
application.body: Real disciples "remain" in His word (verse 31), and agreeing once is not the same as living there. Several who "believed" in verse 30 are trying to kill Him by the end of the chapter.
application.question: Which teaching of Jesus did you once agree with but have quietly stopped living in?

context.heading: Who sinned?
context.body: The disciples assume suffering traces back to someone's sin, a common view that Job's friends also held (Job 4:7). Some Jewish teachers even speculated about sin in the womb. Jesus refuses both options in v. 3. He does not explain all suffering, but He denies that this man's blindness is a verdict on him or his parents.

context.heading: Thrown out of the synagogue
context.body: Aposynagōgos (v. 22) means expelled from the synagogue, and in a village that meant losing worship, friends, family standing and often business. The parents' fear was realistic. Many scholars think John's first readers, late in the first century, knew this pressure firsthand, which may be why the chapter tells the story so fully.

context.heading: A verdict that opens eyes
context.body: "For krima, judgment, I came into this world" (v. 39). Krima is a verdict or decision. Jesus' coming sorts people: the blind who admit their need receive sight, while those who claim to see are left in the dark. It echoes Isaiah's promise to open blind eyes (42:7) and his warning about eyes that will not see (6:9–10).

theology.title: The Creator's hands
theology.body: Jesus makes mud from the ground and puts it on the eyes of a man born blind. Many readers, as early as the second-century teacher Irenaeus, have heard an echo of God forming Adam from the dust (Genesis 2:7). Whether or not John intends that echo, Jesus does what only the Creator can do: He gives a man eyes he never had.

theology.title: Works of God in a hard story
theology.body: Jesus says the blindness happened "so that the works of God might be displayed in him" (v. 3). God does not waste suffering, and He can bring glory out of a life everyone else had written off. The man's healing, and his growing faith under pressure, become a testimony that outlives the controversy.

application.title: One thing I know
application.body: The healed man cannot answer every theological question, but he knows this: "I was blind, now I see" (v. 25). He tells what he knows and stops there.
application.question: What do you know firsthand about what Jesus has done, even if you can't answer every objection?

application.title: Letting someone else take the heat
application.body: His parents knew the truth but said, "Ask him, he is of age" (v. 21). Fear of losing their place made them step aside.
application.question: Where are you letting someone else carry the cost of a truth you also know?

application.title: A person, not a puzzle
application.body: The disciples look at a blind beggar and see a theology question. Jesus sees someone to heal.
application.question: Whose pain have you turned into a debate topic instead of a person to help?

context.heading: A festival about a deliverer
context.body: Enkainia, "Dedication" (v. 22), recalled 164 BC, when Judas Maccabeus rededicated the temple after the Syrian king Antiochus IV defiled it. It celebrated God's rescue through a Jewish hero. In winter, Jesus walks in Solomon's covered colonnade, and the crowd asks Him plainly whether He is the Christ. Hopes for another deliverer ran high.

context.heading: One, but not the same person
context.body: "I and the Father are one" (v. 30) uses hen, the neuter form, "one thing," not the masculine "one person." The Father and the Son are united in nature and work without being merged into a single person. Early Christian writers used this verse against both those who denied Jesus' divinity and those who erased the distinction. The crowd hears the claim clearly and picks up stones.

context.heading: "You are gods"
context.body: Jesus quotes Psalm 82:6, where God addresses Israel's rulers or judges as "gods." Interpreters differ on whether the psalm speaks to human judges or heavenly beings. Either way Jesus argues from lesser to greater: if Scripture can call them gods, how is it blasphemy for the One the Father set apart and sent to call Himself God's Son?

theology.title: Held in two hands
theology.body: No one can harpazō, snatch, Jesus' sheep from His hand, nor from the Father's hand (vv. 28–29). The word that described the crowd trying to seize Him in 6:15 now describes what no enemy can do to His people. Christians differ on whether a true believer can finally fall away, but all affirm that God's keeping power is greater than any outside threat.

theology.title: A death no one could take
theology.body: "No one takes it from Me, but I lay it down of My own accord" (v. 18). Jesus is not a victim swept up by events; He gives His life and has authority to take it up again. His "other sheep" (v. 16) point to Gentiles joining one flock under one shepherd, fulfilling God's promise of one shepherd for His people (Ezekiel 37:24).

application.title: Whose voice is familiar?
application.body: Sheep follow the voice they know and run from strangers (vv. 4–5). Familiarity comes from hours spent listening.
application.question: Which voices in your feed are more familiar to you right now than the voice of Jesus?

application.title: When the wolf shows up
application.body: The hired hand is fine until it gets costly; then he runs (v. 12). Leadership at home, at work or in church is tested on the bad days, not the easy ones.
application.question: Where are you acting like a hired hand who leaves as soon as staying gets expensive?

application.title: What the thief takes
application.body: The thief comes to steal, kill and destroy; Jesus came so His sheep may have life in abundance (v. 10). Some thieves look like rest or entertainment.
application.question: What is quietly stealing life from you that you have been calling a harmless habit?

context.heading: Thomas the Twin
context.body: Thomas is an Aramaic name meaning "twin," and John gives the Greek equivalent, Didymos (v. 16). Thomas is remembered for doubting (20:25), but here he speaks with grim courage: "Let us also go, that we may die with Him." Judea was dangerous, since the leaders had just tried to stone Jesus (10:31). Thomas expects the worst and goes anyway.

context.heading: Quiet tears
context.body: Mary and the mourners are klaiō, weeping aloud in the way of public mourning (v. 33). In v. 35 John uses a different verb for Jesus: dakryō, to shed tears, found only here in the New Testament. Jesus knows He is about to raise Lazarus, and still He weeps beside His friends.

context.heading: Better for one man to die
context.body: Caiaphas argues it is sympherō, "to your advantage," that one man die rather than the nation perish (v. 50). The council fears Rome will take away "our place," probably the temple, and the nation (v. 48). John notes that the high priest spoke better than he knew (v. 51). Within forty years Rome destroyed both anyway, in AD 70.

theology.title: A delay that was love
theology.body: "Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus. So when He heard that Lazarus was sick, He stayed two days longer" (vv. 5–6). The "so" is startling: the delay flows from love, not indifference. God's timing can feel cruel in the moment, yet here it makes room for a greater glory than a healing would have shown.

theology.title: I will open your graves
theology.body: Through Ezekiel God promised, "I will open your graves and raise you from them" (Ezekiel 37:12–13). Jesus calls a four-day-dead man out by name. Lazarus would die again, so this is a preview, not the final event: within days Jesus Himself will rise to a life death can never touch.

application.title: The "if only" sentence
application.body: Martha and Mary both say the same words: "Lord, if You had been here, my brother would not have died" (vv. 21, 32). Jesus answers one with truth and the other with tears.
application.question: What "if only" have you been carrying, and have you ever said it to Jesus directly?

application.title: Unbind him
application.body: Jesus raises Lazarus, then tells the bystanders to take off the grave clothes (v. 44). He gives life; His people help remove what still clings.
application.question: Who near you has new life but is still wrapped in old grave clothes you could help loosen?

application.title: Sacrificing someone for safety
application.body: Caiaphas was willing to let one man pay so the institution stayed secure. It is a calculation offices and families still make.
application.question: Where are you tempted to let someone else take the hit so your own position stays safe?

context.heading: A year's wages poured out
context.body: Mary uses a litra (about 11 ounces) of pure nardos, nard, an aromatic oil imported from the Himalayan region. Judas values it at three hundred denarii (v. 5), roughly a year's wages for a laborer. Some suggest it was a family treasure kept for a dowry or burial. Mary spends it in one act, and the whole house fills with the scent.

context.heading: Hosanna and palm branches
context.body: Hōsanna is Hebrew for "save, please," from Psalm 118:25, a psalm sung at the great festivals. Palm branches had greeted Simon Maccabeus after a military victory (1 Maccabees 13:51), so the crowd may be hailing a liberator. Jesus answers by choosing a young donkey, fulfilling Zechariah 9:9's humble king who comes in peace.

context.heading: The ruler thrown out
context.body: "Now the ruler of this world will be cast out" (v. 31). Archōn means a ruler or official, and John uses it for Satan (14:30; 16:11). At the very moment the cross looks like evil's triumph, Jesus announces it as the devil's eviction. The world's real power is being overturned by a man about to be crucified.

theology.title: Isaiah saw His glory
theology.body: John quotes Isaiah 53:1 and 6:10, then says Isaiah said these things "because he saw His glory" (v. 41). In Isaiah 6 the prophet saw the Lord, high and lifted up, on His throne. John identifies the glory Isaiah saw with the glory of Jesus. The suffering servant and the enthroned Lord are the same person.

theology.title: The Father speaks from heaven
theology.body: When Jesus prays, "Father, glorify Your name," a voice answers, "I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again" (v. 28). The Father openly stands behind the Son's path to the cross. God's name, His revealed character, will be displayed most fully not in a show of force but in His Son's death.

application.title: Criticizing someone else's devotion
application.body: Judas dressed up his complaint as concern for the poor, but John says he was stealing from the money bag (v. 6). Pious objections can hide other motives.
application.question: When someone else's generosity toward God irritates you, what is really under the complaint?

application.title: Troubled and still going
application.body: Jesus admits His soul is troubled and asks whether He should pray to be saved from this hour (verse 27). He feels the dread fully and still does not ask out.
application.question: What hard thing are you praying to escape that you may actually be called to walk through?

application.title: Secret believers
application.body: Many leaders believed but kept quiet for fear of being expelled, because they loved human glory more than God's (vv. 42–43). Their faith was real enough to know, not enough to say.
application.question: Where is your faith genuine but kept silent because saying it would cost you standing?

context.heading: Laying down, taking up
context.body: Jesus "laid aside" His garments (tithēmi) and tied a lention, a linen towel, around His waist (v. 4), the dress of a servant. Afterward He "took" them again (v. 12). John used the same pair of verbs when Jesus said He would lay down His life and take it up again (10:17–18). The foot washing is a small acted picture of the cross.

context.heading: Reclining at His side
context.body: At formal meals guests reclined on couches, leaning on the left elbow, so the person to your right lay close to your chest. The beloved disciple is "at Jesus' side" (kolpos, v. 23), the same word used of the Son at the Father's side in 1:18. This unnamed disciple is traditionally identified as John, son of Zebedee, the Gospel's author (21:24).

context.heading: A morsel of friendship
context.body: A host handing a guest a psōmion, a piece of bread dipped in the dish, was a mark of honor or friendship. Jesus offers it to Judas (v. 26) after quoting Psalm 41:9: "He who ate My bread has lifted his heel against Me." To the end, Jesus treats His betrayer as a guest.

theology.title: Knowing all things, He served
theology.body: Jesus washes feet "knowing that the Father had given all things into His hands" (v. 3). His humility does not come from weakness or insecurity but from full awareness of His authority. This is the shape of God's power, the same pattern Paul describes when the Son took the form of a servant (Philippians 2:6–8).

theology.title: Glory in the dark
theology.body: Judas goes out, "and it was night" (v. 30). Immediately Jesus says, "Now the Son of Man is glorified, and God is glorified in Him" (v. 31). The betrayal that starts the passion is the moment Jesus calls glory. God takes the darkest human act and makes it the stage for His saving love.

application.title: Letting yourself be served
application.body: Peter refuses at first: "You shall never wash my feet" (v. 8). Pride can hide behind humility and still say no to grace.
application.question: Why is it sometimes harder for you to receive help than to give it?

application.title: Judas's feet too
application.body: Jesus washed every pair of feet at that table, including those that would walk out to betray Him. Love here is not a feeling but an action done to a specific person.
application.question: Whose feet would you find hardest to wash this week, and what would it look like to do it?

application.title: The badge outsiders read
application.body: "By this everyone will know that you are My disciples, if you have love for one another" (v. 35). Jesus made the church's relationships its public evidence.
application.question: If people judged Jesus only by how your church treats each other, what would they conclude?

context.heading: A road with a face
context.body: Thomas asks how they can know the way (v. 5). Jesus answers, "I am the way" (hodos, a road or path). Early believers were known simply as people of "the Way" (Acts 9:2). Jesus does not hand His friends a map; He offers Himself as the road to the Father. The claim is exclusive, but He speaks it to comfort grieving friends.

context.heading: Not the peace Rome gave
context.body: "Peace I leave with you" (v. 27) uses eirēnē, the Greek word for the Hebrew shalom: wholeness and well-being, not just quiet. The empire boasted of the Pax Romana, peace enforced by legions. Jesus gives His peace the night before He is executed, and adds, "Do not let your hearts be troubled or afraid."

context.heading: Greater works
context.body: Believers will do "greater works" than Jesus (v. 12). Megas here most likely means greater in reach rather than in power, since no disciple will exceed raising the dead. After Jesus goes to the Father and sends the Spirit, the gospel spreads to thousands at Pentecost and then to the nations.

theology.title: Seen Me, seen the Father
theology.body: Philip asks, "Show us the Father" (v. 8), much like Moses asking to see God's glory (Exodus 33:18). Jesus answers, "Whoever has seen Me has seen the Father" (v. 9). God is not hiding behind Jesus, holding back a different face. What Jesus is, the Father is.

theology.title: The triune God moves in
theology.body: The Son asks, the Father gives, and the Spirit comes to be with believers forever (v. 16). Then the Father and the Son make their home with whoever loves Jesus (v. 23). The chapter is full of the Trinity, not as a puzzle but as a family welcoming people into its life.

application.title: Comfort in a real crisis
application.body: Jesus says "Let not your hearts be troubled" on the worst night of the disciples' lives, not on a calm one. His comfort is meant for real fear.
application.question: Which specific fear would change tonight if you truly believed Jesus is preparing a place for you?

application.title: Love you can check
application.body: "If you love Me, you will keep My commandments" (v. 15). Jesus defines love for Him in terms others could observe.
application.question: Which command of Jesus would your closest friend say you plainly don't keep?

application.title: Three years and still asking
application.body: Philip had walked with Jesus for years and still asked to see the Father. We can be near Jesus and miss what is in front of us.
application.question: Where are you asking God for a sign when He has already shown Himself to you in Jesus?

context.heading: Lifted or cut off?
context.body: The Father airō every fruitless branch (v. 2). The verb can mean "take away" or "lift up." Most translations say "takes away," while some suggest a vinedresser lifting trailing branches off the ground to help them bear. Interpreters also differ on whether fruitless branches are false disciples or believers under discipline; v. 6 makes the warning serious either way.

context.heading: Pruned and clean
context.body: Jesus makes a play on words: the Father kathairō, "prunes," fruitful branches (v. 2), and the disciples are already katharos, "clean," because of His word (v. 3). In Greek the two words sound alike. The same word that cleanses them is the knife that shapes them.

context.heading: Witnesses for the defense
context.body: The Spirit will martyreō, "testify," about Jesus, and the disciples will testify too (vv. 26–27). It is courtroom language. The law required two witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15), and while the world puts Jesus on trial, the Spirit and the church become His witnesses.

theology.title: The vine brought out of Egypt
theology.body: Psalm 80 calls Israel a vine God brought out of Egypt and pleads for the "son of man" whom God made strong (Psalm 80:8, 17). Jesus, the Son of Man, is the true vine, the faithful Israel. God's long story with His people finds its center in a person, and being joined to Him is what makes anyone part of the vine.

theology.title: Chosen to bear fruit
theology.body: "You did not choose Me, but I chose you and appointed you to go and bear fruit" (v. 16). Jesus' friendship begins with His initiative, not ours. Christians understand divine choosing in different ways, but here its purpose is plain: lasting fruit and answered prayer.

theology.title: Love with a measure
theology.body: "Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends" (v. 13). Jesus says it hours before doing it. God's love is not described from a distance; it is demonstrated at a cost.

application.title: When God prunes
application.body: Pruning removes healthy growth too, so the plant's strength goes where it matters. It looks like loss before it looks like fruit.
application.question: What has been cut back in your life recently that you are still treating as nothing but loss?

application.title: Nothing apart from Him
application.body: "Apart from Me you can do nothing" (v. 5). We tend to agree in theory and then run whole areas of life on our own power.
application.question: Which part of your life do you run as if fruit could grow there without Jesus at all?

application.title: Hated for the right reason
application.body: Jesus warns the world will hate His followers as it hated Him "without a cause" (v. 25; Psalm 69:4). Not every rejection is persecution.
application.question: When people push back on you, how do you tell whether it is for following Jesus or for being difficult?

context.heading: A cross-examination
context.body: The Spirit will elenchō the world (v. 8): expose, prove wrong, convict, the way a prosecutor exposes a false witness. The world thought it was judging Jesus. The Spirit will show it was wrong about sin (refusing to believe), about righteousness (Jesus vindicated by going to the Father) and about judgment (the ruler of this world condemned).

context.heading: A guide in unknown country
context.body: Hodēgeō (v. 13) means to lead along the way, like a guide through unfamiliar land; it is related to hodos, "way" (14:6). The promise was first for the apostles, whose Spirit-guided teaching became the New Testament. By extension, Christians trust the same Spirit to lead them into understanding what He has already revealed, not into new revelation that contradicts it.

context.heading: Pressure before birth
context.body: Thlipsis (v. 21) means pressure or crushing distress, here the anguish of labor. The prophets used birth pains for the suffering that comes before God's new age (Isaiah 26:17–19; 66:7–9). Jesus says the disciples' grief will not be replaced by joy but turned into joy, the way labor pain becomes the reason for a mother's delight.

theology.title: The Father Himself loves you
theology.body: "The Father Himself loves you, because you have loved Me" (v. 27). Jesus is not a kind Son persuading a reluctant, angry Father to tolerate His friends. The Father's love is the source of the whole plan of salvation, and through the Son believers can come to Him directly.

theology.title: Better that He goes
theology.body: "It is to your advantage that I go away" (v. 7). The disciples could not imagine anything better than Jesus beside them. But His death, resurrection and ascension make way for the Spirit promised by the prophets (Joel 2:28; Ezekiel 36:27), who will be with every believer everywhere at once.

application.title: Labor pains, not a life sentence
application.body: Jesus does not deny their sorrow; He changes what it means. The pain is real, and it is also leading somewhere.
application.question: What sorrow are you treating as permanent that Jesus might call labor pain?

application.title: Not alone when abandoned
application.body: Jesus predicts His friends will scatter and leave Him alone, then adds, "Yet I am not alone, for the Father is with Me" (v. 32). Abandonment by people did not define Him.
application.question: When people let you down, what keeps you from concluding that you are completely alone?

application.title: More than you can carry now
application.body: "I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now" (v. 12). Jesus paces what He reveals.
application.question: Are you demanding answers from God that you may not yet be ready to carry?

context.heading: Glory that was there before
context.body: Doxazō (v. 1) means to glorify, to make someone's true weight and splendor visible. In John, Jesus is glorified through the cross, resurrection and return to the Father. In v. 5 He asks for the glory He had with the Father "before the world existed," a clear claim that He shared God's glory before creation.

context.heading: Making the name known
context.body: "I have revealed Your name" (v. 6). In Hebrew thought a name (onoma) stands for a person's character and presence. God revealed His name to Moses at the bush and on Sinai (Exodus 3:14; 34:5–7). Jesus says He has now shown the disciples who the Father truly is.

context.heading: The son of destruction
context.body: Judas is called "the son of apōleia" (v. 12), a Hebrew-style idiom meaning someone marked by or headed for destruction. Paul uses the same phrase for the man of lawlessness (2 Thessalonians 2:3). John holds two truths together: Scripture was fulfilled, and Judas was fully responsible for his choice.

theology.title: Love before the world began
theology.body: "You loved Me before the foundation of the world" (v. 24). Before anything was made, the Father loved the Son in the Spirit. Astonishingly, Jesus prays that the world will know the Father has loved His people "even as You loved Me" (v. 23). Believers are drawn into a love older than creation.

theology.title: Unity that mirrors God
theology.body: Jesus prays that believers may be one "just as You, Father, are in Me, and I in You" (v. 21). Christian unity is meant to reflect the unity of God Himself, and its purpose is evangelistic: so that the world may believe. Christians differ on how visible or structural this unity must be, but none can treat division as harmless.

application.title: In the world, not of it
application.body: Jesus does not ask the Father to take His people out of the world but to keep them from the evil one (v. 15). Withdrawal and blending in both miss the point.
application.question: Are you mostly trying to escape the world, blend into it, or actually be sent into it?

application.title: You were prayed for
application.body: Jesus prays for "those who will believe in Me through their word" (v. 20). If you believe, He had you in mind the night before the cross.
application.question: How would your next hard week look different if you remembered Jesus has already prayed for you?

application.title: The unity you avoid
application.body: It is easy to love unity in general and avoid one specific Christian in particular.
application.question: Which believer are you avoiding right now that Jesus prayed you would be one with?

context.heading: Across the Kidron
context.body: Jesus crosses the Kidron Valley east of Jerusalem (v. 1). Centuries earlier King David crossed the same brook weeping as he fled Absalom, betrayed by his trusted counselor Ahithophel (2 Samuel 15:23, 31). The son of David now walks the same path, about to be betrayed by a friend who shared His table.

context.heading: A cohort for one man
context.body: Judas comes with a speira (v. 3), the word for a Roman cohort, nominally several hundred soldiers, though probably a detachment here, along with temple police. They carry torches and lamps on a Passover night lit by the full moon. It is overwhelming force for one unarmed teacher, and at His word they fall back.

context.heading: Careful about the wrong thing
context.body: The leaders will not enter the praitōrion, the Roman governor's headquarters, so that they are not defiled and can still eat the Passover (v. 28). Entering a Gentile residence could make them ritually unclean. They guard their purity while arranging an innocent man's execution. How John's Passover timing fits the other Gospels is debated, with several reasonable proposals.

theology.title: The cup the Father gives
theology.body: "Shall I not drink the cup the Father has given Me?" (v. 11). In the prophets the cup often stands for God's judgment (Isaiah 51:17; Jeremiah 25:15). Jesus receives it willingly, not as a victim of circumstances. The arrest is not the Father losing control but the Son obeying His plan.

theology.title: The shepherd shields His sheep
theology.body: "If you are looking for Me, let these men go" (v. 8). Even while being arrested, Jesus protects His disciples so that His word would be fulfilled: "I have not lost one of those You gave Me" (v. 9). The scene is a small picture of substitution: He is taken, and they go free.

application.title: Put the sword away
application.body: Peter swings a sword to defend Jesus and cuts off Malchus's ear (v. 10). Jesus rebukes him, because zeal can fight for Jesus in ways He never asked for.
application.question: Where are you defending Jesus in a way that does not look anything like Him?

application.title: Warming up with the wrong crowd
application.body: Peter stands with the servants and officers, warming himself at their fire, and denies Jesus there (vv. 18, 25). Where we stand shapes what we say.
application.question: In which setting is it easiest for you to quietly act as if you don't belong to Jesus?

application.title: Clean hands, dirty plans
application.body: The leaders kept the purity rule and broke the weightier law of justice. Small scruples can sit comfortably beside large sins.
application.question: What religious detail are you careful about while ignoring something far heavier?

context.heading: The day of Preparation
context.body: John notes it was the paraskeuē, "Preparation," of the Passover, "about the sixth hour" (v. 14), around noon, close to when Passover lambs began to be slaughtered in the temple that afternoon. John's timing presents Jesus as the true Passover lamb. Mark 15:25 mentions the third hour for the crucifixion, and scholars offer various explanations, such as approximate or different ways of reckoning time.

context.heading: A tunic woven from the top
context.body: The soldiers divide His clothes but cast lots for His chitōn, the long inner tunic, because it was seamless, woven in one piece "from the top" (v. 23), the word anōthen from 3:3. This fulfills Psalm 22:18. Some readers also connect it with the high priest's woven robe (Exodus 28:32), though John does not say so directly.

context.heading: Blood and water
context.body: When a soldier pierces Jesus' side, "blood and water" flow out (v. 34). Whatever its exact medical explanation, the detail confirms He truly died, against later teachers who denied a real death (1 John 5:6). The eyewitness insists on it (v. 35). Many readers also see an echo of the living water (7:38) and the life-giving blood (6:54) Jesus promised.

theology.title: They will look on Me
theology.body: John cites Zechariah 12:10: "They will look on the One they have pierced" (v. 37). In Zechariah, it is the Lord Himself speaking: "they will look on Me." The pierced man on the cross is the God of Israel, wounded by His own people and pouring out grace on them. With Psalm 22, Psalm 69 and Exodus 12:46, Scripture converges on this hill.

theology.title: Power given from above
theology.body: Pilate boasts that he has authority to free or crucify, and Jesus replies, "You would have no authority over Me if it were not given to you from above" (v. 11). God rules even over an unjust trial, yet that does not excuse anyone: the one who handed Jesus over has the greater sin. Sovereignty and responsibility stand side by side.

application.title: No king but Caesar
application.body: The chief priests, guardians of Israel's faith in God as King, end up shouting, "We have no king but Caesar" (v. 15). Fear of losing position led them to crown the wrong ruler.
application.question: What earthly security have you quietly crowned king in your life?

application.title: Care from the cross
application.body: In agony, Jesus makes sure His mother will be cared for (vv. 26–27). Responsibility for the people who depend on us does not pause when life gets heavy.
application.question: Who depends on you that you are tempted to neglect when your own pressure rises?

application.title: Secret disciples step out
application.body: Joseph and Nicodemus, both quiet followers, publicly ask for the body when the movement looks finished (vv. 38–39). They chose the worst moment to be seen.
application.question: What would it look like for you to identify with Jesus openly when it is least convenient?

context.heading: Called by name
context.body: Mary does not recognize Jesus until He says her name; then she answers, "Rabbouni" (v. 16). It is Aramaic for "my teacher" or "my master," a warmer and more personal form than "rabbi." The good shepherd "calls his own sheep by name" (10:3), and here one of them knows His voice.

context.heading: Stop holding on
context.body: "Do not cling to Me" (v. 17) uses haptomai in a form that often means "stop holding on." Jesus is not forbidding touch, since He later invites Thomas to touch Him (v. 27). He is telling Mary that the old way of being with Him is ending. He is going to the Father, and a new relationship is beginning.

context.heading: He breathed on them
context.body: Emphysaō, "breathed on" (v. 22), is the verb the Greek Old Testament uses when God breathed life into Adam (Genesis 2:7) and when breath came into the dry bones (Ezekiel 37:9). The risen Jesus is beginning a new creation. Christians explain the relation of this moment to Pentecost (Acts 2) in different ways.

theology.title: My Father and your Father
theology.body: Jesus sends word to "My brothers": "I am ascending to My Father and your Father, to My God and your God" (v. 17). Through His death and resurrection, His followers are brought into God's family. Yet He still says "My" and "your" separately: His sonship is eternal, theirs is a gift of grace.

theology.title: Written so you may believe
theology.body: John says he wrote these signs so that readers "may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in His name" (v. 31). God does not ask for a blind leap. He gives eyewitness testimony and signs, and invites faith grounded in what really happened.

application.title: Behind locked doors
application.body: The disciples locked themselves in out of fear, and Jesus came and stood among them anyway, saying, "Peace be with you" (v. 19). Locked doors did not keep Him out.
application.question: What fear are you locking the doors against, and will you let Jesus into that room?

application.title: Doubt in the room
application.body: Thomas doubted, but a week later he was still with the other disciples when Jesus came (v. 26). He brought his questions into the community instead of walking away with them.
application.question: When you doubt, do you take it away from other believers or into the room with them?

application.title: Sent like He was sent
application.body: "As the Father has sent Me, I also send you" (v. 21). Jesus' mission becomes the pattern for ours.
application.question: If Jesus sent you the way the Father sent Him, where in your ordinary week would that start?

context.heading: Hauling in the catch
context.body: Peter "hauled" (helkō) the net ashore, full of 153 large fish (v. 11). It is the verb Jesus used for the Father drawing people (6:44) and for Himself drawing all people (12:32). The exact number reads like a fisherman's careful count; many symbolic meanings have been proposed, but none is certain. What is clear is that the net did not tear.

context.heading: Feed My lambs
context.body: Jesus answers each of Peter's replies with a task: boskō, "feed" (v. 15), and poimainō, "shepherd" (v. 16). One stresses providing food, the other the whole work of guiding and protecting. Peter later urges church leaders to "shepherd the flock of God" (1 Peter 5:2), passing on what he received on this beach.

context.heading: Another will dress you
context.body: When Peter was young he would zōnnymi, fasten his own belt, and go where he wanted; when old, he would stretch out his hands and another would dress him (v. 18). John explains it signals how Peter would die (v. 19). Early Christian tradition says he was crucified in Rome under Nero, around AD 64.

theology.title: The God of second callings
theology.body: Three questions answer three denials, and the scene ends with "Follow Me" (v. 19), the same words that began the disciples' story (1:43). The God who restored Israel after its unfaithfulness restores Peter by name. Failure is not the end of a calling when Jesus is the one who renews it.

theology.title: A testimony that is true
theology.body: "We know that his testimony is true" (v. 24). The Gospel closes by rooting itself in an eyewitness, the beloved disciple, confirmed by a community that knew him. God's revelation comes through real history and reliable witnesses. And the last verse admits that no number of books could hold all that Jesus did.

application.title: Back to the boats
application.body: Unsure what came next after the resurrection, Peter says, "I am going fishing" (v. 3). Old routines feel safe when the future is unclear.
application.question: When you don't know what God wants next, which old routine do you run back to by default?

application.title: What about him?
application.body: Peter hears his own future and immediately asks about John's (v. 21). Jesus replies, "What is that to you? You follow Me."
application.question: Whose calling are you comparing yours to, and what would change if you stopped?

application.title: Love with a job attached
application.body: Every time Peter says he loves Jesus, Jesus gives him people to care for. Love for Christ goes to work on His sheep.
application.question: If you told Jesus today that you love Him, whose needs do you think He would point you toward first?
